stories.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
stories.summary: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities By James Landale Reporting from Zaporizhzhia oblast Published 15 September 2026 Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way. His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb. But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta. And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present. "If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can." Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. It was defeated on Thursday at the UN Security Council by a vote of 11-2, with Somalia and Pakistan abstaining.The UN Security Council sanctions, which were reimposed on 27 September last year under the snapback mechanism of the 2015 nuclear deal, remain in effect. stories.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
stories.summary: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mhsg A drone view of flood damage along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot district, Nepal. Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing . The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26. "This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone." That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises. This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin. Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair. But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say. "We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently. That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story? Far from it. For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. stories.article_text_excerpt: At one of the biggest financial forums in Central Asia, Euronews moderated a panel focusing on Kazakhstan drive to turn its position at the heart of Eurasia into more than a transit advantage, by developing logistics, manufacturing and investment.Infrastructure investor Nurzhan Marabayev said efficient, transparent and competitive logistics could unlock new projects across Central Asia. Kazakhstan has relatively low labour, resource and construction costs, he noted, but expensive logistics remain a challenge for the landlocked country.Airport director Meruyert Zholdybayeva highlighted the potential of multimodal transport, citing a China-Europe route that moves goods from Shenzhen to Europe in seven days. She said Aktau could eventually become a major hub combining rail, sea and air links.Manufacturing is also expanding. Alima Issembayeva said production rose from 2.3 trillion tenge in 2021 to almost 4 trillion in 2025, while exports more than doubled between 2021 and 2024.Trade expert Ilya Urazakov cited Kazakhstan’s FDI record and natural resources as key advantages, while Professor Tom Vinaimont stressed the need for currency hedging and predictable financing.
